summary: Describes principles of Internet host configuration, covering Internet-layer parameters as well as those that affect higher-layer protocols. It offers guidance for designing configuration mechanisms.

plainLanguage.summary: When you get a new computer, it needs settings before it can use the network. This note explains good rules for how a computer should get those settings.

questions: what principles should guide host configuration design
should configuration be tied to the link layer
how do you configure hosts securely
subtitle: Guidance for designing systems that automatically give computers their network settings.

tldr.problem: Computers need network settings to operate on the Internet, but configuration mechanisms are often complex and error-prone. There are many different ways to configure hosts, creating interoperability and maintenance problems.
tldr.mechanism: This document presents five core principles: minimize configuration, keep mechanisms simple, reduce the number of different configuration approaches, make configuration independent of the underlying link layer, and separate configuration from access control.
tldr.outcome: These principles help protocol designers avoid misconfiguration errors and reduce the burden on both administrators and embedded devices. The document recommends relying on general-purpose mechanisms like DHCP rather than inventing new configuration approaches.

facts.label: Internet-layer parameters
facts.value: IP addresses, subnet prefixes, default gateways, mobility agents, boot service configuration

facts.label: Higher-layer parameters
facts.value: DNS servers, NTP servers, service discovery information

today: RFC 5505 is Informational and remains a reference for protocol designers working on host configuration mechanisms. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Need for Host Configuration
sections.content: Internet hosts require configuration to operate: an IP address, a subnet mask, a default gateway address, DNS server addresses, and many other parameters. Configuration involves both Internet-layer parameters (addresses, gateways, routing) and higher-layer parameters (DNS, NTP, service discovery). The document addresses architectural questions about which protocol layer should handle each kind of configuration, how configuration relates to service discovery, and how to avoid security and interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer needs to know its own address, where to send messages, and how to find servers. This section explains what settings are needed and why designing good ways to deliver them is tricky.

sections.title: Five Core Principles
sections.content:
Minimize configuration. Anything that can be configured can be misconfigured. Parameters should be automatically computed or have reasonable defaults whenever possible. Long lists of configurable options increase the risk of human error. Where configuration is necessary, protocols should support self-configuration through capability negotiation or automated discovery.

Less is more. Simple, standardized mechanisms are essential for devices with limited resources, like embedded systems and preboot environments. A complex configuration mechanism may be too large to fit in a device's boot ROM.

Minimize diversity. Multiple host configuration mechanisms create interoperability problems (a host may not support the mechanism available on a given network), increase device footprint (hosts must implement all mechanisms they might encounter), add latency, and may create conflicting configurations that require complex merge logic.

Lower-layer independence. Configuration mechanisms should work the same way regardless of the underlying link type (Ethernet, PPP, wireless, tunnels). Link-layer-specific configuration adds complexity and makes it difficult to support new link types. Internet-layer mechanisms like DHCP are preferable to implementing configuration within each link-layer protocol.

Configuration is not access control. Network access authentication is a separate problem from configuration. Authentication should not be a prerequisite for obtaining IP address configuration parameters, since users can often configure hosts manually anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: The five rules are: (1) let computers figure out settings themselves, (2) keep the system simple, (3) use the same approach on all networks, (4) do not tie configuration to the type of cable or wireless used, and (5) do not confuse getting a network address with allowing access to the network.

sections.title: Configuration Versus Service Discovery
sections.content:
Configuration mechanisms like DHCP provide a small list of interchangeable servers (such as a few DNS servers or time servers) that are relatively static and learned once at boot time. Service discovery protocols, by contrast, help applications find a server matching specific criteria (a fast color printer nearby, a file server with available storage) and can adapt as the network changes.

Configuration of a few well-known servers is appropriate for interchangeable services. Listing hundreds of printers in DHCP is less useful because users only need one printer on a given day. Service discovery protocols can support discovery beyond the local link and adapt to dynamic changes, but they typically cannot be relied upon for basic Internet-layer configuration because they may need a Directory Agent address, which must itself be configured.

The document also discusses fate sharing: when configuration information is obtainable only if the server providing it is available and the information is usable only if that server is available, the mechanism has good fate sharing. Router Advertisements provide perfect fate sharing; configuring a name to discover a DNS server also provides fate sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: Configuration gives a host a small list of helper servers it learns at startup time. Service discovery helps applications find specific servers as they need them. These are different problems that need different solutions.

sections.title: Dual-Stack and Multi-Interface Challenges
sections.content:
Hosts that support both IPv4 and IPv6 face new challenges. When configuring server addresses, it is desirable to obtain both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in a single combined list, ordered by expected success probability. Obtaining them separately requires the host to guess which IPv4 and IPv6 addresses belong to the same server, which risks suboptimal fallback behavior if the first address fails.

Configuration of many parameters occurs on a per-interface basis (via DHCP on each interface), but the configuration affects host-wide behavior (a host has one DNS resolver, not one per interface). The document recommends that protocol specifications include guidance on how to merge per-interface configurations into coherent host-wide settings, including decisions about selection versus union of configurations and prioritization rules.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer has multiple network connections or supports both IPv4 and IPv6, it needs to combine the settings from each connection intelligently so everything works together.

sections.title: Configuration Security and Authentication
sections.content:
Securing IP configuration is difficult because a host without an IP address has very limited networking capabilities and cannot use security facilities like IPsec or TLS. Configuration security is typically implemented within the configuration protocols themselves rather than below the IP layer.

Techniques include filtering (access points can drop DHCP offers from clients), IPsec protection of DHCP relay-to-server communication, SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) for IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration, and DHCP authentication (though adoption is limited). Stateless DHCPv6 can be secured with IPsec. Boot configuration deserves special attention because a successful attack can give an attacker complete control of the host. When public key cryptography is used, hosts must be pre-configured with trust anchors to validate configuration messages, which is challenging for nomadic hosts visiting multiple administrative domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Protecting configuration messages is hard because a computer cannot use encryption until after it has its network address. Different approaches include filtering bad messages, protecting relay servers, and using cryptographic signatures on configuration data.
